query: How To Not Run Out of Cash as a Founder: 2 Things That Really, Really Help
answer:
So I want to just talk to founders on how to make sure they don't run out of cash. There are two things that really help, two that will always work if you do 'em well enough, if you do 'em consistently. But like most advice, there's also some nuance here. The first thing I'm going to tell you to do is create four to five crisp, clear business objectives for the year. Now, why would we even care? Why does that matter? It matters because almost everyone in your team is going to forget what their goal was by week three. Everyone knows what they need to do every day, but very few people know where they're actually going longer term than maybe six months. And so when folks hear "four to five key objectives," they say, "Oh yeah, I already got those. My boss told me." Well, let me challenge you with a little bit different way of thinking about it. When you go into a board meeting and someone asks you — and probably you'll get asked this in a VCs' board meeting later, too — "What are your top four objectives?" You should literally look up at him, smile and say, "Well, Bob, I've got my slides right over here. Let me show you."
And then you pull them up and you clearly present each of those four to five objectives. What did you achieve in the prior quarter? Where do you stand today? And where do you hope to end up? This forces you to think about it. Even if it doesn't force you to put it together, it forces you to think through all the important stuff. Now, I know some folks might say, "Hey, isn't this just like our OKR framework?"
It is similar.

Dear SaaStr: What Are the 5 Things Every Founder Should Know In the Early Days?
My list:
Slow it down if you don’t have a great co-founder
. Another idea will come, but it’s almost impossible to thrive without an amazing co-founder.  More
here

You always need about 25% more than your raise
. So always raise 25% more than you think you need, even in an angel round. But don’t spend that 25%. Maybe even put it in a different business bank account.  A bit more
here
.
You’ll lose a year to a truly terrible VP hire
. They’ll hire an entire terrible team, your revenue will slow, and they’ll spend a ton of money doing it. You are better off with No VP than a bad one.  More

Competition doesn’t kill you
. Not having a 10x feature kills you. Giving up kills you. But even the best competitors don’t try to win in every segment of the market. And even the best competitor doesn’t have 100% market share.  More

.

Is Your Best Leverage
Buyers can sense desperation when you’re running out of money. Smart investors give companies “breathing room” during sales processes because a healthy balance sheet dramatically improves your negotiating position. Running out of cash creates terrible leverage and often leads to unfavorable terms. Maintaining financial stability throughout the process gives you the option to walk away – the most powerful negotiating tool of all.
Honest Self-Assessment Determines Success
The hardest questions to answer honestly: Are you truly gaining market share? Do you have a genuinely great team? What’s your unit economics reality? Companies like Shopify and HubSpot IPO’d at valuations under $1B and now are worth $143B and $38B respectively – could your company follow a similar trajectory? This honest assessment determines whether selling is actually the right move. If you’re gaining market share with a great team and solid unit economics, you may never need to sell.
Founder Burnout Is a Real Factor
Many acquisitions happen around the 5-year mark when founders get tired and a decent offer appears tempting. The hard work of overcoming initial inertia is complete, and the prospect of a significant liquidity event becomes increasingly attractive. Before making permanent decisions, consider taking a three-week break or sabbatical. The power of recurring revenue is extraordinary – businesses can grow from $1M to $250M monthly even after being somewhat neglected if the underlying model is sound. Think carefully before selling what might become your legacy.
The decision to sell your company represents one of the most consequential choices a founder will make. By approaching the process with clear eyes and realistic expectations, you dramatically increase your chances of an outcome you won’t regret. Remember that patience is a luxury not all founders have, but those who can maintain it often see the greatest rewards.
